exercise_group.instructions: The statements in Exercises 1–19 refer to vectors in $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ (or $\textbf{ℝ}^{m}$) with the standard inner product. Mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer.

statement.paragraph: (T/F) The length of every vector is a positive number.
(T/F) A vector $\mathbf{v}$ and its negative, $- \mathbf{v}$, have equal lengths.
(T/F) The distance between $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ is $\parallel \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} \parallel$.
(T/F) If $r$ is any scalar, then $\text{∥}r\mathbf{v}\text{∥} = r\text{∥}\textbf{v}\text{∥}$.
(T/F) If two vectors are orthogonal, they are linearly independent.
(T/F) If $\textbf{x}$ is orthogonal to both $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$, then $\textbf{x}$ must be orthogonal to $\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}$.
(T/F) If $\text{∥}\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}\text{∥}^{2} = \text{∥}\textbf{u}\text{∥}^{2} + \text{∥}\textbf{v}\text{∥}^{2}$, then $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are orthogonal.
(T/F) If $\text{∥}\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}\text{∥}^{2} = \text{∥}\textbf{u}\text{∥}^{2} + \text{∥}\textbf{v}\text{∥}^{2}$, then $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are orthogonal.
(T/F) The orthogonal projection of $\textbf{y}$ onto $\mathbf{u}$ is a scalar multiple of $\textbf{y}$.
(T/F) If a vector $\textbf{y}$ coincides with its orthogonal projection onto a subspace $W$, then $\textbf{y}$ is in $W$.
(T/F) The set of all vectors in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ orthogonal to one fixed vector is a subspace of $\text{ℝ}^{n}$.
(T/F) If $W$ is a subspace of $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$, then $W$ and $W^{\bot}$ have no vectors in common.

(T/F) If $\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{2}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{3} \right\}$ is an orthogonal set and if $c_{1}$, $c_{2}$, and $c_{3}$ are scalars, then $\left\{ c_{1}\mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,~}c_{2}\mathbf{v}_{2}\text{,~}c_{3}\mathbf{v}_{3} \right\}$ is an orthogonal set.
(T/F) If a matrix $U$ has orthonormal columns, then $UU^{T} = I$.
(T/F) A square matrix with orthogonal columns is an orthogonal matrix.
(T/F) If a square matrix has orthonormal columns, then it also has orthonormal rows.
(T/F) If $W$ is a subspace, then $\parallel \text{proj}_{W}\mathbf{v}\text{∥}^{2} + \text{∥}\mathbf{v} - \text{proj}_{W}\mathbf{v}\text{∥}^{2} = \text{∥}\textbf{v}\text{∥}^{2}$.

(T/F) A least-squares solution of $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$ is the vector $A\widehat{\textbf{x}}$ in $\text{Col~}A$ closest to $\textbf{b}$, so that $\parallel \textbf{b} - A\widehat{\textbf{x}} \parallel \leq \parallel \textbf{b} - A\textbf{x} \parallel$ for all $\textbf{x}$.
(T/F) The normal equations for a least-squares solution of $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$ are given by $\widehat{\textbf{x}} = \left( A^{T} A)^{- 1}A^{T}{\textbf{b}} \right.$.

Let $\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,~}\ldots\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{p} \right\}$ be an orthonormal set. Verify the following equality by induction, beginning with $p = 2$. If $\textbf{x} = c_{1}\mathbf{v}_{1} + \cdots + c_{p}\mathbf{v}_{p}$, then $\left. \text{∥}\textbf{x}\text{∥}^{2} = \middle| c_{1} \middle| {}_{2} + \cdots + \middle| c_{p} \right|^{2}$

Let $\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,~}\ldots\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{p} \right\}$ be an orthonormal set in $\textbf{ℝ}^{n}$. Verify the following inequality, called Bessel’s inequality, which is true for each $\textbf{x}$ in $\textbf{ℝ}^{n}$:

Let $U$ be an $n \times n$ orthogonal matrix. Show that if $\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,~}\ldots\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{n} \right\}$ is an orthonormal basis for $\textbf{ℝ}^{n}$, then so is $\left\{ U\mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,~}\ldots\text{,~}U\mathbf{v}_{n} \right\}$.

Show that if an $n \times n$ matrix $U$ satisfies $(U\textbf{x}) \cdot (U\textbf{y}) = \textbf{x} \cdot \textbf{y}$ for all $\textbf{x}$ and $\textbf{y}$ in $\textbf{ℝ}^{n}$, then $U$ is an orthogonal matrix.
Show that if $U$ is an orthogonal matrix, then any real eigenvalue of $U$ must be $\pm 1$.

A Householder matrix, or an elementary reflector, has the form $Q = I - 2\textbf{uu}^{T}$ where $\mathbf{u}$ is a unit vector. Show that $Q$ is an orthogonal matrix. (Elementary reflectors are often used in computer programs to produce a QR factorization of a matrix $A$. If $A$ has linearly independent columns, then left-multiplication by a sequence of elementary reflectors can produce an upper triangular matrix.)

Let $T:\textbf{ℝ}^{n}\rightarrow\textbf{ℝ}^{n}$ be a linear transformation that preserves lengths; that is, $\parallel T\left( \textbf{x} \right) \parallel = \parallel \textbf{x} \parallel$ for all $\textbf{x}$ in $\textbf{ℝ}^{n}$.

list.item: Show that T also preserves orthogonality; that is, T(x)⋅T(y)=0 whenever x⋅y=0.
Show that the standard matrix of T is an orthogonal matrix.

statement.paragraph: Let $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ be linearly independent vectors in $\textbf{ℝ}^{n}$ that are not orthogonal. Describe how to find the best approximation to $\textbf{z}$ in $\textbf{ℝ}^{n}$ by vectors of the form $x_{1}\mathbf{u} + x_{2}\mathbf{v}$ without first constructing an orthogonal basis for $\text{Span~}\left\{ \mathbf{u}\text{,~}\mathbf{v} \right\}$.

Suppose the columns of $A$ are linearly independent. Determine what happens to the least-squares solution $\widehat{\textbf{x}}$ of $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$ when $\textbf{b}$ is replaced by $c\textbf{b}$ for some nonzero scalar $c$.

If $a$, $b$, and $c$ are distinct numbers, then the following system is inconsistent because the graphs of the equations are parallel planes. Show that the set of all least-squares solutions of the system is precisely the plane whose equation is $x - 2y + 5z = (a + b + c)/3$.
Consider the problem of finding an eigenvalue of an $n \times n$ matrix $A$ when an approximate eigenvector $\mathbf{v}$ is known. Since $\mathbf{v}$ is not exactly correct, the equation

will probably not have a solution. However, $\lambda$ can be estimated by a least-squares solution when (1) is viewed properly. Think of $\mathbf{v}$ as an $n \times 1$ matrix $V$, think of $\lambda$ as a vector in $\textbf{ℝ}^{1}$, and denote the vector $A\mathbf{v}$ by the symbol $\textbf{b}$. Then (1) becomes $\textbf{b} = \lambda V$, which may also be written as $V\lambda = \textbf{b}$. Find the least-squares solution of this system of $n$ equations in the one unknown $\lambda$, and write this solution using the original symbols. The resulting estimate for $\lambda$ is called a Rayleigh quotient.
Use the steps below to prove the following relations among the four fundamental subspaces determined by an $m \times n$ matrix $A$.
﻿$\text{Row~}A = \left( \text{Nul~}A \right)^{\bot},\text{Col~}A = {\text{(Nul~}A^{T}\text{)}}^{\bot}$﻿

list.item: Show that Row A is contained in (Nul AT)⊥. (Show that if x is in Row A, then x is orthogonal to every u in Nul A.)
Suppose rank A=r. Find dimNul A and dim(Nul A)⊥, and then deduce from part (a) that Row A=(Nul A)⊥. [Hint: Study the exercises for Section 6.3.]

statement.paragraph: Explain why an equation $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$ has a solution if and only if $\textbf{b}$ is orthogonal to all solutions of the equation $A^{T}\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$.

exercise_group.instructions: Exercises 33 and 34 concern the (real) Schur factorization of an $n \times n$ matrix $A$ in the form $A = URU^{T}$, where $U$ is an orthogonal matrix and $R$ is an $n \times n$ upper triangular matrix.1

statement.paragraph: Show that if $A$ admits a (real) Schur factorization, $A = URU^{T}$, then $A$ has $n$ real eigenvalues, counting multiplicities.

Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ matrix with $n$ real eigenvalues, counting multiplicities, denoted by $\lambda_{1}$, $\ldots$, $\lambda_{n}$. It can be shown that $A$ admits a (real) Schur factorization. Parts (a) and (b) show the key ideas in the proof. The rest of the proof amounts to repeating (a) and (b) for successively smaller matrices, and then piecing together the results.

list.item: Let u1 be a unit eigenvector corresponding to λ1, let u2, …, un be any other vectors such that {u1, …, un} is an orthonormal basis for ℝn, and then let U=[u1u2⋯un]. Show that the first column of UTAU is λ1e1, where e1 is the first column of the n×n identity matrix.
Part (a) implies that UTAU has the form shown below. Explain why the eigenvalues of A1 are λ2, …, λn. [Hint: See the Supplementary Exercises for Chapter 5.]UTAU=[λ1****0⋮A10]

statement.paragraph: [T] When the right side of an equation $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$ is changed slightly—say, to $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b} + \text{Δ}\textbf{b}$ for some vector $\text{Δ}\textbf{b}$—the solution changes from $\textbf{x}$ to $\textbf{x} + \text{Δ}\textbf{x}$, where $\text{Δ}\textbf{x}$ satisfies $A\left( \text{Δ}\textbf{x} \right) = \text{Δ}\textbf{b}$. The quotient $\parallel \text{Δ}\textbf{b} \parallel \text{/} \parallel \textbf{b} \parallel$ is called the relative change in $\textbf{b}$ (or the relative error in $\textbf{b}$ when $\text{Δ}\textbf{b}$ represents possible error in the entries of $\textbf{b}$). The relative change in the solution is $\parallel \text{Δ}\textbf{x} \parallel \text{/} \parallel \textbf{x} \parallel$. exercises.instructions: 1 If complex numbers are allowed, every$n \times n$ matrix $A$ admits a (complex) Schur factorization, $A = URU^{- 1}$, where $R$ is upper triangular and $U^{- 1}$ is the conjugate transpose of $U$. This very useful fact is discussed in Matrix Analysis, by Roger A. Horn and Charles R. Johnson (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1985), pp. 79–100.
